top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: This systematic review included 65 sources in the qualitative synthesis, consisting primarily of contemporary pediatric ERCP primary studies and selected prior systematic reviews or meta-analyses used for contextual benchmarking[2-14, 19-71]. Prior reviews were not treated as independent primary data and their pooled estimates were not combined with overlapping primary studies. A detailed account of the literature screening and selection process, following PRISMA 2020 principles, is illustrated in Figure 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: The methodological quality and risk of bias of each eligible source were independently assessed by two reviewers using tools appropriate to study design. Disagreements were resolved by consensus, with a third reviewer consulted when needed. Non-randomized primary studies were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), randomized trials using RoB 2, and prior systematic reviews or meta-analyses using AMSTAR 2[16-18]. Rather than reproducing checklist content, we summarized each study's overall judgment and used these judgments to grade confidence across evidence domains. Risk-of-bias judgments informed the narrative synthesis. Studies with incomplete adverse-event definitions, unclear denominators, overlapping cohorts, or high risk of selection or reporting bias were interpreted cautiously and were not used to support quantitative claims beyond their reported data.

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to identify, pool, and stratify reported post-ERCP adverse events in pediatric patients. Two reviewers independently searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for literature on pediatric ERCP complications. Any discrepancies in study selection were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords using Boolean operators (AND, OR). Keywords included: 'children', 'pediatric', 'ERCP', 'endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography', 'complications', 'adverse event', 'pancreatitis', 'bleeding', 'perforation', and 'infection'. The search was limited to studies published between January 1, 2015, and June 26, 2025, to capture contemporary pediatric ERCP practice, including changes in therapeutic indications, endoscopic accessories, anesthesia support, and prophylaxis strategies. Earlier evidence was considered through prior reviews only for contextual comparison. Reference lists of eligible studies and relevant reviews were manually checked to identify additional contemporary primary studies. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies were selected using predefined criteria: Inclusion Criteria: Study Type: Original pediatric studies, including cohort studies, case-control studies, and randomized or nonrandomized interventional studies. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were screened for contextual comparison and citation tracking only. Their pooled results were not entered into the present quantitative synthesis. Population: Pediatric patients (<18 years) undergoing ERCP. Outcomes: Reported incidence, types, risk factors, or management strategies of post-ERCP complications. Language: English. Publication Date: January 1, 2015 to June 26, 2025. ARTICLE IN PRESS Exclusion Criteria: Population: Adult patients (≥18 years). Intervention: Research unrelated to ERCP complications. Study Design: Case reports, narrative reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, animal studies, in vitro studies. Data Availability: Incomplete or unextractable data. Duplication: Repeated publications.

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was conducted only for outcomes reported by at least three non-overlapping primary studies with extractable numerators and denominators. Pooled incidences were estimated using random-effects models for proportions, with variance stabilization for rare events where appropriate. Results were expressed as pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran Q and the I-squared statistic. Heterogeneity was interpreted as low, moderate, substantial, or considerable using conventional thresholds, while acknowledging that I-squared may be unstable in rare-event analyses. We prespecified subgroup exploration by age group, ERCP indication, procedure type, pancreatic duct manipulation or contrast injection, sphincterotomy, and operator or center volume. Formal subgroup meta-analysis was not forced when studies did not provide stratified PEP event counts, because doing so would have required ecological assumptions. These variables were therefore summarized as explanatory domains for heterogeneity and risk. Sensitivity analyses were planned by excluding studies at high risk of bias, studies with unclear adverseevent definitions, and studies with potential cohort overlap. In response to peer review, we also added a post hoc denominator-unit sensitivity summary, separating procedure-level studies from patient-level or first-ERCP-perchild studies and retaining a mixed/unclear category when the source did not permit classification. Risk-factor effect estimates were not pooled when exposure definitions, covariate adjustment, or reporting units differed substantially. These data were summarized narratively and, where appropriate, displayed as reported estimates. ARTICLE IN PRESS Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots and statistically using Egger test only for outcomes with at least ten eligible studies. Funnel plots were not generated for rare outcomes with fewer than ten studies because asymmetry tests would be unreliable. All tests were two-sided. For analyses other than Cochran's Q test for heterogeneity, P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For Cochran's Q test, P < 0.10 was considered indicative of potential between-study heterogeneity because this test has limited power when relatively few studies are included. Heterogeneity was interpreted together with I² and τ². AI-assisted tools were used during revision for language editing and formatting checks. The authors verified the data extraction, statistical analyses, interpretation, and final text and take full responsibility for the manuscript.

top_evidence.text: Most included primary studies were retrospective or observational, and the overall certainty of evidence was limited by heterogeneous adverse-event definitions, variable follow-up windows, incomplete reporting of denominators for specific complications, and potential overlap among multicenter pediatric ERCP cohorts. Contemporary multicenter studies generally provided stronger evidence for technical outcomes and common adverse events, whereas estimates for rare events such as perforation and cholangitis were less precise. Prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses were useful for benchmarking but were not used as data sources in the present pooled analyses.

top_evidence.text: Data extraction was independently conducted by two reviewers using a standardized form. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. For each primary study, we collected first author, year, country, study design, sample size, number of ERCP procedures, mean or median age, ERCP indications, procedure type, follow-up duration, adverse-event definitions or reporting windows, event numerators and denominators for PEP, bleeding, perforation, cholangitis or infection, severity classification, risk factors, and management strategies. For PEP, we recorded whether the denominator represented ERCP procedures, patients, first ERCP per child, or a mixed/unclear reporting unit. We retained the denominator unit used by the source rather than converting procedure-level data to patient-level data when repeat procedures per child were not consistently reported.
